content: The relationship between high-density lipoprotein (HDL) concentration and cardiovascular outcomes, particularly in statin-treated high-risk patients with residual cardiovascular risks, has garnered significant interest in the evaluation of HDL-lowering drugs. HDL is one of the most complex and heterogeneous lipoproteins, with its subfractions varying significantly in function, structure, size, and cholesterol and triglyceride content. The most commonly used method for measuring HDL is based on the chemical quantification of HDL-cholesterol (HDL-C). However, recent evidence suggests that HDL-C may not be the most accurate measure of HDL functionality or its association with cardiovascular outcomes in statin-treated patients. Emerging studies propose that HDL-particles (HDL-P) may serve as a better indicator of HDL's role in residual cardiovascular risk. HDL is highly heterogeneous in terms of its structure, size, and the proportion of cholesterol and triglycerides it contains. Different HDL subtypes exhibit distinct physicochemical and functional characteristics. While several studies have demonstrated an inverse relationship between HDL-C levels and cardiovascular risks, this association has not been consistently observed. This inconsistency may be due to the fact that HDL-C levels do not necessarily reflect the actual functionality of HDL. Consequently, it has been hypothesized that HDL-C may not be the optimal metric for assessing HDL functionality or its relationship with cardiovascular risk factors. HDL-P refers to the total concentration of all HDL subfractions. It can be measured using nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy or ion mobility analysis. However, these two methods do not yield identical results, and there is currently no standardized modality for measuring HDL-P. A study published in September 2013, based on data from the JUPITER trial (Justification for the Use of Statins in Primary Prevention: An Intervention Trial Evaluating Rosuvastatin), suggested that HDL-P might be a superior tool for assessing HDL levels and their association with residual cardiovascular outcomes in statin-treated patients. This study measured HDL size, HDL-P, HDL-C, and apolipoprotein A-I levels in 10,886 participants. Among statin-treated individuals, HDL-P was more strongly associated with coronary vascular disease than HDL-C. In contrast, in patients not treated with statins, HDL-P and HDL-C were equally correlated with coronary vascular disease. The MESA trial (Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis) reported that lower HDL-P levels were associated with increased carotid artery intima-media thickness (cIMT), a marker of atherosclerosis. After adjusting for LDL-P and other factors, HDL-C was no longer associated with cIMT, whereas HDL-P remained significantly associated. Identifying an accurate clinical method to measure HDL is of critical importance, especially as numerous trials investigating new HDL-raising therapies are ongoing. Few studies have evaluated the relationship between HDL-P and coronary heart disease (CHD) risks, and none have jointly assessed HDL-P, HDL-C, and LDL-P. The MESA study demonstrated that HDL-C's association with cIMT and CHD incidence was substantially attenuated after adjusting for atherogenic lipoproteins, particularly LDL-P. In contrast, HDL-P's associations with cIMT and CHD incidence were relatively unaffected by adjustments for atherogenic lipoproteins, HDL-C, or mean HDL particle size. The MRFIT (Multiple Risk Factor Intervention Trial) found that low HDL-P levels predicted CHD death over 18 years of follow-up among men with metabolic syndrome. High levels of HDL-P, particularly medium-sized HDL-P, were associated with a reduced risk of CHD. Similarly, the EPIC-Norfolk study showed that lower HDL-P levels predicted incident cardiovascular events independently of age, sex, apoB, triglycerides, mean HDL particle size, smoking, myeloperoxidase, paraoxonase-1, and hsCRP. In the VA-HIT (Veterans Affairs High-Density Lipoprotein Intervention Trial), lower baseline and on-trial HDL-P levels predicted CHD events among men with low HDL-C randomized to gemfibrozil versus placebo. The Women's Health Study demonstrated an inverse association between HDL-P and incident cardiovascular disease over 11 years of follow-up, though this was not statistically significant. However, in the Women's Health Initiative Hormone Trial, HDL-P was inversely associated with incident CHD among postmenopausal women, adjusted for treatment arm. Additionally, the inverse association of HDL-P with cIMT was statistically significant in women in the current study. Various modalities are available for measuring HDL, including covalent chromatography, chemical precipitation, cross-immune electrophoresis, ion mobility assays, NMR, one-dimensional gel electrophoresis, and ultracentrifugation. Chemical measurements can estimate HDL concentrations in blood samples, but they may not reflect the functional capacity of HDL particles to reverse cholesterol transport from tissues. HDL-C is measured by removing LDL particles through aggregation or precipitation with divalent ions (e.g., Mg++) and coupling the products of a cholesterol oxidase reaction to an indicator reaction. Measuring apo-A reactive capacity can also be used to assess HDL cholesterol, though it is considered less accurate. Electrophoresis measurements, utilized since the 1960s, take advantage of HDL particles' net negative charge and size variability to indicate particle number and sort them by size. Larger HDL particles carry more cholesterol. The newest methodology for measuring HDL particles, available clinically since the late 1990s, uses NMR fingerprinting to measure both concentration and size. This technique, pioneered by Jim Otvos and a North Carolina State University research spinoff company, has significantly reduced the cost of HDL measurements.
